title: Social-media restrictions can erode when compliance is socially costly
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35162; Australian teenagers surveyed after the national under-16 social-media account restriction
geography: Australia; comparative mechanism test for U.S. youth-platform policy

observations.period: Four months after the December 2025 restriction; 14–15-year-olds

denominator.unit: Australian teenagers in the reported survey sample

compliance.unit: percent; approximate share of 14–15-year-olds complying with the restriction

peer_threshold.unit: percent of peers respondents reported would need to comply before they would comply

perceived_status.value: Compliers were perceived as less popular than non-compliers

observations.method: Post-policy survey of Australian teenagers, with reported compliance, perceived peer behavior, perceived popularity, and stated peer threshold; the study interprets the restriction through a coordination/tipping-point framework.
observations.uncertainty: The sample is Australian and age-specific; self-reported compliance and perceived peer behavior may contain reporting or perception error. The study does not identify individual causal effects on mental health, school outcomes, or family life.
observations.subgroup: Australian teenagers, especially 14–15-year-olds subject to the restriction; estimates should not be generalized to all adolescents or platforms.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low compliance may reflect enforcement design, circumvention, platform-specific use, or pre-existing norms rather than a general failure of age restrictions. A reported threshold is not a revealed behavioral threshold.

observations.period: Two months after the initial post-policy survey

denominator.unit: follow-up compliance estimate; source summary does not disclose a separate respondent count

direction.value: compliance declined from the initial post-policy level

observations.method: Reported follow-up observation in the NBER study after the initial post-policy survey; the public summary describes the direction and approximate share but not a full follow-up denominator.
observations.uncertainty: The follow-up estimate is not a disclosed national compliance rate and should not be treated as a causal time-series estimate without the underlying panel, attrition, and measurement details.
observations.subgroup: The study's affected Australian adolescent population; follow-up composition and retention are not fully specified in the public summary.
observations.counterinterpretation: The decline could reflect sample composition, enforcement changes, reporting changes, or platform substitution; it does not prove that all age restrictions will erode.

related_sources.claim: The research brief reports the 746-teen sample, approximate one-quarter compliance, and the two-thirds peer threshold.
Accessible working-paper abstract for the reported post-policy and follow-up mechanism.

boundary: This comparative record shows a policy-to-compliance-to-social-norm mechanism in an Australian youth-platform setting. It does not establish U.S. compliance, mental-health benefit, school effect, family burden, privacy improvement, durable exit, or political legitimacy. Formal restriction, actual behavior, peer norms, wellbeing, and later action remain separate stages.
